title: Totem Marine Tug & Barge, Inc. v. Alyeska Pipeline Service Co.
lead: A new tug-and-barge company accepted a sharply reduced settlement while claiming imminent bankruptcy; evidence that its customer knowingly withheld an acknowledged debt required a trial on economic duress.

actors.name: Totem Marine Tug & Barge, Inc.
actors.role: New Alaska carrier and settlement challenger

actors.name: Alyeska Pipeline Service Company
actors.role: Pipeline customer terminating the voyage contract and invoking the release

actors.name: Richard Stair and Pacific, Inc.
actors.role: Financiers and coplaintiffs; Stair signed for Totem

actors.name: Justice Burke
actors.role: Author of the Alaska Supreme Court opinion

proceedings: Superior court granted summary judgment on executed release; Supreme Court corrected exclusion of deposition material, reversed, and remanded for trial on disputed duress facts.
limits: The allegations were sufficient for trial, not proven duress. The Court neither rescinded the release nor found termination wrongful nor awarded the contract balance. Stair and Pacific had no separate original-contract rights merely because they did not sign the release.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Totem’s first contract encountered cargo and voyage delays
sections.cue: Introduce the shipping arrangement and the disputed loading account.
paragraphs: Totem Marine Tug & Barge began operating in March 1975. Its first contract, made in June with Alyeska Pipeline Service Company, required transporting construction materials from Houston to a southern Alaska port, possibly collecting more cargo en route, with completion around August 15. Totem chartered the Marine Flasher barge and Kirt Chouest tug using loans and guarantees from Richard Stair and his company Pacific, Inc.

According to Totem’s summary-judgment evidence, Alyeska represented roughly 1,800–2,100 tons of ordinary uncoated pipe in Houston and possible later cargo of 6,000–7,000 tons. Instead Houston held some 6,700–7,200 tons of coated pipe, beams, and valves improperly stacked. Modifications, extra cranes, and stevedores became necessary, and loading took thirty days instead of the three Totem expected for 2,000 tons. Payment assurances, weather, and administrative difficulties added delay; the heavy load slowed progress. These were disputed assertions, not final trial findings.

sections.title: A second tug and an interrupted delivery preceded termination
sections.cue: Trace the events potentially relevant to later financial pressure.
paragraphs: With Alyeska’s verbal consent, Totem chartered the N. Joseph Guidry as a second tug on August 13. When it reached the Panama Canal without a written amendment, Stair directed it not to pass. Alyeska signed the amendment August 21 after further disputes. The tug lost preferred passage and waited another two or three days. Once the vessels joined, a hurricane’s tail impeded them another eight or nine days.

Near San Pedro, Totem planned refueling and a crew change, but Alyeska directed the vessels to Long Beach. Totem alleged unloading began without permission or necessary surveys, voiding its insurance. After disputes and concessions the cargo came off, and Alyeska terminated around September 14, reaffirming days later without explaining why. The Supreme Court later reserved whether termination was wrongful.

Totem submitted termination invoices totaling about $260,000–$300,000. An Alyeska official reportedly said review might produce payment in a day or in six to eight months. Totem’s debts came due on ten-to-thirty-day schedules, creditors demanded payment, and Stair said cash was needed immediately to avoid bankruptcy.

sections.title: Counsel negotiated a $97,500 release under the asserted cash crisis
sections.cue: Follow execution, suit, and the deposition-record problem.
paragraphs: Totem told attorney Roy Bell to explain its financial situation to Alyeska. Bell negotiated in Seattle, Alyeska offered $97,500, and Stair signed a release of all Totem claims for that amount on November 6. The opinion uses differing officer titles for Stair; he acted for Totem.

Totem, Stair, and Pacific sued March 26, 1976. The amended complaint sought rescission for economic duress, the unpaid balance, and compensatory and punitive damages for alleged wrongful termination. Before answering, Alyeska moved for summary judgment on the release. Totem alleged deliberate withholding of acknowledged debt with knowledge of looming bankruptcy; Alyeska disputed it. The superior court granted judgment November 30.

Both sides had relied heavily on Stair’s deposition, but it was not formally opened and presented. After appeal began, the superior court refused to publish it as part of the record. The Supreme Court held it at least had to consider passages identified in memoranda and argument. To avoid another limited remand, it examined those portions itself and denied Alyeska’s request to strike related reply-brief references. It did not consider Cooke’s separate deposition because neither side relied on its contents on appeal.

sections.title: Economic duress required wrongful pressure and no reasonable alternative
sections.cue: Explain the standard without making distress alone sufficient.
paragraphs: Justice Burke’s opinion addressed an Alaska issue not previously decided. Duress had expanded beyond threats to body or liberty toward economic coercion and attention to the particular person induced, while contract freedom and settlement finality remained important. Financial disadvantage or reluctance alone could not invalidate a bargain.

The claimant needed wrongful oppressive conduct causing involuntary assent without a reasonable alternative, not merely its own necessities. Wrongfulness depended on context and could extend beyond criminal or tortious conduct. Bad-faith threats to breach or withhold an admitted debt could qualify.

Alternatives might include suit, replacement goods or services, or other funds, but adequacy was practical. A judgment arriving after immediate irreparable business collapse might not suffice. Austin Instrument and Gallagher illustrated unavailable timely substitutes threatening contractors’ government work; Capps concerned a small settlement accepted to avert foreclosure and repossession. Those examples did not mean every distressed creditor lacked alternatives.

sections.title: The summary-judgment record raised issues without satisfying a trial burden
sections.cue: Identify the unresolved facts and role of legal counsel.
paragraphs: If proved, deliberate withholding of acknowledged payment while Alyeska knew bankruptcy left no practical alternative could establish duress. Acknowledgment need not cover every invoiced dollar, but roughly the claimed amount. Wrongful termination itself was not essential, though earlier conduct could illuminate coercion.

Alyeska initially met its summary-judgment burden through the signed release, legal representation, and Stair’s understanding. Totem then needed competent, specific evidence, not just allegations, but did not yet have to prove ultimate success. The trial court demanded too much by emphasizing Stair’s lack of direct negotiation and Bell’s absence as a witness. The Supreme Court considered the showing weak and Bell’s testimony probably necessary to prevail, yet sufficient with favorable inferences to require trial.

Questions remained whether Alyeska acknowledged a particular debt, bankruptcy was imminent, Alyeska knew the financial condition, and words or conduct threatened withholding unless Totem settled. Counsel and knowing execution mattered but did not conclusively defeat practical compulsion.

sections.title: Reversal reopened the release dispute without creating independent claims
sections.cue: End with the financiers’ position and the actual remedy.
paragraphs: Stair and Pacific separately argued they were not bound because they had not signed the release. Neither had been a party to the shipping contract or amendment, and neither asserted third-party-beneficiary status. They therefore had no independent contractual claim to avoid releasing; their position depended on Totem’s success or failure.

On August 25, 1978, Burke, Chief Justice Boochever, Rabinowitz, Connor, and Matthews unanimously reversed and remanded for trial. They did not find duress, rescind the settlement, decide termination wrongfulness, or award unpaid invoices. The actual release was $97,500 against invoices around $260,000–$300,000, distinct from rounded figures in the later instructional problem.

sources.pinpoint: Id. at 15, 17, 19, 24–25; assigned Financial Stress problem
